html:
A rush of about 100,000 people toward the Klondike region of the Yukon in northwestern Canada, after gold was found on Bonanza Creek in August 1896. The finders were the American George Carmack and his Tagish relatives Skookum Jim and Dawson Charlie.

News reached Seattle and San Francisco in July 1897, when ships arrived carrying miners and their gold, and set off a stampede. The trip was brutal. Most people landed at Skagway or Dyea in Alaska and hauled their supplies over the steep Chilkoot or White passes, then built boats to float down the Yukon River. Canadian police required each person to bring about a year's worth of food. Only about 30,000 to 40,000 made it to Dawson City, which suddenly grew into a city.

Most found that the good claims were already taken, and few grew rich. By 1899 gold was found at Nome, Alaska, and the crowds left. The rush brought the Yukon a government of its own and helped open Alaska, after earlier rushes in California and the Australian colony of Victoria. Writers like Jack London made it a legend.
